passage: Monday. Tejas squeezed glitter glue all over his drawing of a cat, and it smeared into a silver puddle. He frowned and pushed the sheet away. Wednesday. He took a fresh sheet and drew the cat in pencil first. "Glue is last," he told Dilnaz, who sat next to him. Friday. On the card for Nani's birthday the cat stayed clean, and only the border sparkled. Dilnaz leaned over. "Can I do mine like that?" Tejas showed her the pencil, then the glue, in that order.

qa.q: What did Tejas draw on the fresh sheet before using any glue?
qa.a: He drew the cat in pencil first.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when the glitter glue smeared over his cat?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and upset, shown by his frown and by pushing the sheet away.

qa.q: What could Tejas do next time to learn about the glue without risking his card, and why?
qa.a: He could test the glitter glue on a scrap of paper first. He would see how far it spreads before putting it near his drawing.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see Tejas's new way of working?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees a neat, sparkling card and wants the same result, so asks to copy the order of pencil and then glue.

grounding: A smudged drawing leads the child to try pencil first on a fresh sheet and glitter only at the border, learning an order for materials.

passage: Maria had one clean sheet left, and the party was at four. Her first card lay ruined on the table: glitter glue had run into the cat she drew, and her fingers had dragged it into a silver smear. Maria's lip wobbled. Sarita, her big cousin, said, "Only one more paper, Maria." Maria sat very still. Then she picked up a pencil, not the glue. She drew the cat lightly, then the words "Happy Birthday" in pencil too. Only when that was done did she squeeze glitter, carefully, around the edges like a frame. Nothing smeared this time.

qa.q: How many clean sheets did Maria have left?
qa.a: Maria had one clean sheet left.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she looked at her first card?
qa.a: Her wobbling lip shows she was upset and disappointed that the glitter glue had smeared her cat.

qa.q: What else could Maria try to keep the glitter from spoiling a drawing?
qa.a: She could let the glitter dry before touching the card or keep her hand on a scrap sheet; drawing first and adding glitter last already solved most of it.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Maria's second try?
qa.a: Sarita had warned there was only one paper, so she might feel relieved and impressed that Maria slowed down and got it right.

grounding: Shows a child learning from a smeared glitter mess to draw in pencil first and add glitter only around the border.

passage: In their Pune flat, Neelam was making a card for Sarika from the fourth floor. She drew a big cake and squeezed gold glitter glue on the candles straight away. When she reached for a crayon to colour the cake, her wrist swept through the wet gold. The cake turned into a shiny blur. "Mamma, it's spoiled!" Neelam looked at the mess, then at her sparkly wrist. "The sparkly goes last," she decided. She took a fresh page, drew the cake in pencil, coloured it, and put glitter only around the edge. This time she kept her hand far away while it dried.

qa.q: What did Neelam use to draw the cake on the fresh page?
qa.a: She drew the cake in pencil, then coloured it.

qa.q: What does Neelam's cry of 'it's spoiled' show about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt upset and frustrated when her wrist turned the cake into a shiny blur.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were helping Neelam next time?
qa.a: Keep the glitter glue out of reach until the drawing and colouring are done, which is the order she worked out herself.

qa.q: What would change for Sarika if Neelam had given up after the first card?
qa.a: Sarika would have got no card at all, or a blurry one; because Neelam changed the order, Sarika gets a neat cake with a gold edge.

grounding: Illustrates a child using a glitter smudge as a lesson to draw in pencil first and add glitter only at the border.
